one_liner: Table-less software CRC-32 using sparse zero polynomials; about 2x zlib 1.3.1.1's braided CRC on large buffers.
what_it_does: This is the reference code for the arXiv paper: a set of C functions that compute the IEEE/gzip CRC-32 of a buffer. The bulk loop uses no lookup tables and no carry-less-multiply or CRC instructions. Every variant has the signature uint32_t f(uint32_t crc, char* buf, size_t len); chorba_standard calls chorba_118960_nondestructive for inputs of 238,432 bytes or more and chorba_small_nondestructive below that. An optional chorba_pclmul applies the idea to an x86 PCLMUL/AVX folding loop. The repo is a benchmark harness (test_crc plus zlib submodules), not a library, and the maintained form of the algorithm is zlib-ng 2.3+, where it is built by default (WITH_CRC32_CHORBA=ON).
how_it_is_fast: A zero polynomial Z(x) satisfies Z(x) mod G(x) = 0, so XORing it into the message leaves the CRC unchanged. Choosing one with few terms, such as x^14870 + x^22 + x^11 + x^7 + 1 with exponents scaled from bits to 64-bit words, cancels each input word by XORing shifted copies of it into a few words roughly 118.8-119 KB further ahead (hence the variant name 118960). The main loop is then plain 64-bit shifts and XORs, with no table loads and no serial dependency on the CRC register. Non-destructive variants keep these forward contributions in a 128 KiB power-of-two ring buffer (the wrap is a bitmask); destructive variants XOR them straight into the caller's buffer. The last ~72 bytes go through a 256-entry Sarwate table, and on x86 the same shift/XOR steps are interleaved between PCLMUL folds.
when_to_use: You need a portable C CRC-32 for buffers of about 240 KB or more on 64-bit CPUs where CLMUL/PMULL or CRC32 instructions are unavailable or not allowed. At 16-256 MiB the paper's plots show chorba_118960_nondestructive at roughly 2.2x (Ryzen 5 5600) and 3x (Graviton2, Raspberry Pi 4) the throughput of zlib 1.3.1.1 braiding (plot readings are approximate).

Cortex-A72-class boards such as the Raspberry Pi 4. The paper calls the non-destructive 118960 variant the best performer there, and its plot shows it at or slightly ahead of zlib's native-CRC32-instruction path for 16 MiB and larger.
You already link zlib-ng 2.3.2 or later. You get Chorba automatically as the fallback ahead of braiding, with the bug fixes applied, which is better than copying this repo.
You checksum data you own and can overwrite, as in cksum-style tools. On Ryzen and Graviton2 the destructive variants ran close to, or at, the hardware-accelerated reference speed in the plots.
You want reference code for porting the zero-polynomial idea to other CRC widths; the paper lists CRC-32-XFER and CRC-64-ISO as future work.
when_not_to_use: Your CPU has CRC32 or carry-less-multiply instructions you can use. On Graviton2, zlib's native-CRC32 path plotted at ~55-75 s/TiB against ~150 for the best non-destructive Chorba, and the Chorba+PCLMUL tweak adds only 5-20%. The abstract's 'on par with hardware' claim holds in the plots only for some variants and CPUs.
Your messages are small. Below 238,432 bytes everything falls back to chorba_small, which is only ~1.15x braiding at 64 KiB on the Ryzen plot, and the README says braiding is faster below 256 bytes.

You would ship this repo's code in production. It is stale (last commit 2024-12-27) and has no correctness tests. Its 118960 variant still zeroes the ring buffer with a '+ 60' bound; zlib-ng changed that to '+ 64' in PR #2033 to fix wrong CRCs at lengths such as 615,336 bytes (zlib-ng #2029, shipped in the 2.3.2 hotfix).

You target big-endian or 32-bit systems. The code does little-endian 64-bit loads with no byte-swapping. zlib-ng needed a big-endian fix (#1891) and a separate 32-bit small variant; this repo has neither.

You care about memory or per-call cost, or run on a Pi-class memory system. Each large non-destructive call mallocs and zeroes 128 KiB, which the paper says outweighs the gains for smaller messages. The 733112 variants run ~1.5x (destructive) and ~2.4x (non-destructive) slower than braiding on the Raspberry Pi 4 plot.

integration.dependencies: none for the CRC functions themselves, except that the caller must define the 256-entry `crc32_table` they reference as extern (test_crc.h supplies it); the benchmark harness needs the zlib_braiding and zlib_slicing submodules, and the latter uses an SSH (git@github.com) URL
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; C99-style C that the Makefile hard-codes to gcc -O3 (version unstated), with -mno-avx on x86-64; chorba_pclmul needs GCC/Clang `#pragma GCC target("pclmul,avx")` and x86intrin.h
integration.platforms: generic variants assume a 64-bit little-endian CPU (tested on x86-64 Ryzen, Graviton2 aarch64 and Raspberry Pi 4); chorba_pclmul needs x86-64 with PCLMULQDQ and AVX; configure calls lscpu, so the build is Linux-oriented; the AVX2/AVX-512 variants benchmarked in the paper are not in the repo
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each call keeps its state in locals and a per-call malloc'd buffer and only reads the global table, so calls look reentrant, but destructive variants overwrite the caller's buffer
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — produces the same CRC-32 as zlib's crc32(), but the signature is (uint32_t, char*, size_t) with no header. The functions work on the raw register without zlib's ~ pre/post conditioning (the harness wraps zlib as crc32(crc ^ 0xffffffff, ...) ^ 0xffffffff for comparison). zlib-ng 2.3+ is the real drop-in.

gotchas: Conditioning differs from zlib: the functions take and return the un-inverted register, so a standard CRC-32 is f(0xFFFFFFFF, buf, len) ^ 0xFFFFFFFF. Passing a zlib-style running CRC directly gives wrong results.
The *_destructive variants overwrite the input buffer. Only the *_nondestructive variants and chorba_standard leave the data intact.

Loop indices are `int` while len is size_t, so a single call over 2 GiB overflows. Loads are unaligned type-punned `*(uint64_t*)` casts, which is alignment and strict-aliasing UB in ISO C (zlib-ng's port feeds the unaligned head through braid first). The 128 KiB malloc is not NULL-checked.

'Table-less' describes only the bulk loop: the tail (up to ~72 bytes) still uses a 1 KiB Sarwate table. The harness prints the CRC but never compares it with zlib, so the repo does not verify correctness.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued CRC siblings (corsix fast-crc32, dougallj's M1 PMULL code, crc32fast, crc-fast, klauspost/crc32, komrad36/CRC, htot crc32c) get their headline numbers from CLMUL/PMULL or CRC32 instructions and win by a wide margin wherever those exist. Pick Chorba, preferably through zlib-ng, only for the no-hardware-assist case, where it is the fastest portable C CRC-32 in the catalog relative to zlib's braiding.
verified_claims_summary: A single-author arXiv v1 preprint timed 1,000 iterations of IEEE CRC-32 over xorshift buffers on an AMD Ryzen 5 5600, an AWS t4g.micro (Graviton2) and a Raspberry Pi 4. Builds used gcc -O3 (version unstated), and the baseline was zlib 1.3.1.1's braided crc32(). Results exist only as seconds-per-TiB plots: the text lists sizes up to 512 MiB, but the plots stop at 256 MiB. They show the best non-destructive variant at roughly 2.2x braiding on Ryzen and about 3x on the two ARM systems at 16 MiB and above, which is consistent with the abstract's '100%'. A separate 5-20% gain is claimed for grafting the method onto AVX1 PCLMUL folding.
status_note: Stale research code (last commit 2024-12-27, 6 stars) under the permissive zlib license, fine to copy but unmaintained and missing later fixes. Use zlib-ng 2.3.2+ (WITH_CRC32_CHORBA on by default) for a maintained, bug-fixed version.
